video_title: Let There Be Germicidal Light: This $500 Fixture Could Stop the Next Pandemic, from Complex Systems
gist: Aerolamp CEO Misha Gerovich and chief scientist Vivian Balenkei tell Patrick McKenzie that 222nm far-UVC germicidal lighting is technically and commercially ready today at ~$500/lamp, with a credible path to ~$100/lamp with zero new technology, yet global sales are perhaps only a few hundred units per year. Their core claim is that the binding constraint is neither cost, regulation, nor safety science but sheer awareness and social diffusion, and that the largest value is not preventing colds but 'decapping' a future respiratory pandemic by pushing R0 below 1 in transport hubs and congregate spaces.

insights.claim: 222nm far-UVC delivers the airborne-pathogen equivalent of 30 to 50 air changes per hour in a room, versus the one or two extra air changes a conventional ventilation upgrade buys.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp and Columbia University researcher
insights.so_what: The efficacy gap versus ventilation retrofits is roughly an order of magnitude, which is the quantitative basis for far-UVC displacing HVAC spend in large, densely occupied spaces.
insights.quote: instead of maybe giving you an an extra air change or two in your space, you can get the equivalent of 30 to 50

insights.claim: Far-UVC safety is a mechanical rather than biological story: the 20-micron layer of dead, protein-rich skin cells in the stratum corneum absorbs essentially all 200-235nm UVC before it reaches the basal skin cell layer where DNA damage would matter.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The mechanism is wavelength-specific, so safety evidence for 222nm does not transfer to legacy 254nm UVC products and vice versa — a product-differentiation moat and a diligence checkpoint for anyone underwriting a UV company.
insights.quote: humans have a 20 micron thick layer of dead skin cells that are chalk full of proteins that essentially absorb all UVC

insights.claim: The eye is the binding safety constraint for far-UVC because the tear layer absorbs only about 15% of the incident dose, making the safe effective eye dose lower than the safe skin dose and still not precisely pinned down by industry practice.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Ocular dose limits are the most likely place a future standard tightens; one-year and three-year eye safety studies running in Japan are the near-term catalysts to watch.

insights.claim: Far-UVC overexposure is self-limiting in a way infrared laser exposure is not, because pain triggers a flinch response before long-term damage accrues.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Self-limiting failure modes lower product liability exposure and are why the technology can be sold as consumer-installable rather than requiring certified technicians.
insights.quote: With RUV if you if you feel something stop looking at it you know.

insights.claim: There is no UVC in sunlight at all — it is fully blocked by the ozone layer — so the intuition that far-UVC is 'just sunlight indoors' is wrong; sunlight is only mildly germicidal per photon and works by sheer volume.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Marketing the technology as 'natural' is unavailable; the pitch has to be engineered novelty, which is part of why diffusion is slow.

insights.claim: Emitters run at roughly 100 milliwatts, low enough that dose falls to near zero across the length of a room, which is why a low-power fixture can be both germicidally effective and occupant-safe.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Low power draw means no electrical service upgrade is required, removing a major retrofit cost line that plagues HVAC-based alternatives.

themes.theme: Unit economics and the cost curve

insights.claim: Aerolamp prices at $500 per lamp against competitors selling comparable far-UVC fixtures at $2,000 and even $3,500 each, a spread the CEO attributes to tiny incumbents needing high margins to survive rather than to any fundamental cost floor.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: A 4-7x price umbrella held up only by subscale incumbents is the classic setup for a volume entrant to take the category; incumbent far-UVC pricing is not defensible.
insights.quote: a lot of the lamps in this market are being sold for like 2,000. I recently heard someone sell their lamps for 3500 each.

insights.claim: The Aerolamp CEO believes the price of a far-UVC lamp could fall to roughly $100 within the next couple of years with zero technological innovation, purely from volume and margin compression.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: If true, the addressable market inflects at a price point where home and small-business purchase becomes rational, which is the single biggest swing factor in the category's TAM.
insights.quote: I don't think there's any reason that in the you know near future next couple years or so or or even sooner that that the price couldn't be no on the order of a hundred bucks per lamp and that's you know with zero technological innovation of any sort

insights.claim: Coverage math is about 250 square feet per lamp, implying two to four lamps per classroom, dozens per school, and hundreds of lamps for a university-scale install.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete units-per-building multiplier for sizing institutional deal values: small buildings four to five figures, large institutions six figures on lamps alone.

insights.claim: Professional installation roughly doubles the total cost of a far-UVC deployment, making labor about 50% of installed cost in the US — a component that does not compress with manufacturing scale.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Hardware deflation only halves total project cost, so the labor-heavy cost structure caps how much price declines alone can accelerate adoption.
insights.quote: usually we say u installation will cost you probably about what the lamps will cost you if you're hiring professionals to do it

insights.claim: Because 222nm is innately safe, any general electrician can install it, versus legacy upper-room UVC where a botched install causes rapid eye damage and requires a specialist UV installer.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Removing the specialist-installer bottleneck is what makes mass rollout labor-feasible; it is the structural reason UVC failed to scale since the 1940s and 50s.

insights.claim: Current far-UVC emitters are rated for at least 10,000 hours at 70% output — possibly 13,000 to 14,000 hours — giving five to six years of life at office-hours use or about eighteen months running 24/7.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Replacement cycles of 1.5-6 years imply a recurring consumables revenue stream on top of the fixture sale, and make 24/7 venues like airports and train stations the highest-lifetime-value customers.

insights.claim: The host's general rule that anything that fits in a shipping container from China craters in price over time is applied to far-UVC as the reason it should eventually cost little more than ordinary lighting, unlike medical interventions afflicted by Baumol cost disease.
insights.speaker: Patrick McKenzie, host
insights.so_what: Reframes far-UVC as a manufactured good on a hardware deflation curve rather than a healthcare service on an inflation curve — a very different long-run margin and adoption profile.
insights.quote: everything that fits on a shipping container from without loss of generality China um craters in price over time particularly as you scale up production of it

insights.claim: The best far-UVC emitters are made by a single Japanese company operating a high-margin, high-end product business, so even at zero margin the per-unit emitter cost is $15-20.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Single-supplier concentration in Japan is the category's key supply risk and a possible entry point for a second-source manufacturer or a Chinese scale-up play.
insights.quote: we're still looking at a per unit cost of like 15 20 bucks per emitter

insights.claim: Krypton chloride excimer lamps sit on a less aggressive cost curve than LEDs and will likely never reach white-LED pricing, because they require hydrogen fluoride gas in manufacturing rather than the capital-intensive-but-infinitely-replicable chip process.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Tempers the 'LED cost curve' analogy that far-UVC bulls lean on; the real long-run bet is on solid-state chip-based far-UVC emission, which is not commercially near.
insights.quote: these krypton chloride ecimer lamps are on a different less aggressive cost curve. I don't think they could get as cheap as the white LED

insights.claim: Aerolamp is an open-source hardware company that publishes its CAD files on GitHub so anyone can manufacture their own far-UVC fixture.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Deliberately forgoing design IP signals the company is optimizing for category growth over capture — which means the investable margin in this space likely sits in emitters and installation, not fixture design.
insights.quote: we're also an open source company so in principle you know anyone can just uh take the CAD files published on our GitHub and you know make their own

themes.theme: Adoption bottleneck is awareness, not cost or regulation

insights.claim: Worldwide far-UVC lamp sales may be as low as a couple of hundred units per year, meaning the category is not merely early on the adoption curve but arguably not on the curve at all.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: A few hundred units a year against a plausible market of tens of millions is the sharpest quantification in the episode of how much optionality is unpriced in this category.
insights.quote: I think worldwide maybe a couple thousand of these lamps are are sold uh every No, I don't think it's even that high. It might be as low as just a couple of hundred a year worldwide.

insights.claim: There is no regulatory barrier and no missing critical safety study blocking far-UVC deployment — the constraint is purely social diffusion and awareness, which the chief scientist calls the thing that keeps her up at night.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Investors who assume a hidden regulatory or scientific reason for non-adoption are mispricing the category; the actual risk is marketing execution, a far cheaper problem to solve.
insights.quote: there's nothing, you know, super critical where it's like, ah, we just need to know this and then we can get going. And there's not really any regulatory barrier either. It's, you know, it's maybe just like a social diffusion question.

insights.claim: Almost nobody has heard of 222nm even among people already familiar with UV disinfection, and the CEO argues a global awareness or marketing campaign would benefit the world more than almost any other intervention in this space.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Points philanthropic and venture capital toward demand creation rather than R&D — a category where the highest-leverage dollar is a marketing dollar, not a lab dollar.
insights.quote: I think just information is the main bottleneck.

insights.claim: The host publicly bet that the US would have broad far-UVC deployment by 2030 and now expects to lose that bet because the current pace is far too slow.
insights.speaker: Patrick McKenzie, host
insights.so_what: A calibrated forecaster marking down his own timeline is the cleanest available signal that near-term revenue in this sector will disappoint versus the technology's merits.
insights.quote: I once made a bet with someone that we would have a broad deployment to this in the United States by uh 2030 and I think I'm going to lose that bet unfortunately because we're not moving at quite that at that speed.

insights.claim: Realistic deployment timing is anchored to LED lighting's diffusion — at least a decade after real takeoff — compounded by the roughly ten-year commercial building renovation cycle.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The renovation cycle sets the physical clock on institutional penetration; any thesis assuming faster-than-LED adoption needs a specific reason why.

insights.claim: ASHRAE 241 is currently the only infection prevention standard in existence, is still under construction, and is not yet broadly adopted by any authority having jurisdiction — but if it were written into building codes, far-UVC would win by default as the cheapest way to meet the clean-air requirement.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Code adoption by states or counties is the single highest-leverage catalyst for the sector; track AHJ adoption of ASHRAE 241 as the trigger for a step-change in demand.
insights.quote: right now we only have one infection prevention standard that's ashray 241 and it is an amazing standard that was put together very quickly uh but it's still under construction

insights.claim: Too much celebrity attention too early could backfire, so the chief scientist prefers trial deployments and organic normalization in SF, Berkeley, and DC group houses and event spaces over a viral marketing push.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Management is explicitly choosing slower, more robust diffusion over a growth spike — relevant to anyone modeling a hockey-stick revenue ramp.
insights.quote: we are maybe early enough that um too like too much attention could be you know have have something of an IFS effect. So we want to like scale responsibly.

insights.claim: If picking a celebrity endorser, the CEO would choose Paris Hilton over Taylor Swift specifically so that high-end hotel brands become associated with clean air.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Signals hospitality as an underappreciated beachhead vertical where clean air can be sold as a luxury amenity rather than a health cost.
insights.quote: if I was going to pick a celebrity, it wouldn't be Taylor Swift. I think it would be Paris Hilton because if if high-end hotel brands get associated with clean air, I think that would be pretty valuable.

themes.theme: Where evidence and adoption land first

insights.claim: A South African trial in tuberculosis wards using guinea pigs exposed only via shared air with human patients is already showing preliminary 90% transmission suppression.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: This is the strongest real-world efficacy datapoint in the category and the anchor number any commercial pitch will lean on until an RCT exists.
insights.quote: There's a trial going on in South Africa that already has preliminary results and there they're seeing 90% transmission suppression in these in these TP wards.

insights.claim: Tuberculosis is roughly ten times more resistant to far-UVC than a typical respiratory virus like flu or coronavirus, which makes the 90% TB suppression result a conservative rather than optimistic read-across.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The hardest-to-kill pathogen showing the best field result is an asymmetric upside argument — but it is offset by the caveat that TB's transmission dynamics differ from flu's.
insights.quote: tuberculosis is actually not very sensitive to FR UBC at all. It's relatively resistant. Um and I would say it's about maybe 10 times more resistant than your typical respiratory virus like flu or corona virus.

insights.claim: Efficacy evidence will accumulate fastest in low-social-mixing, high-pathogen-load settings — TB hotspot institutions, long-term care and senior centers, and boarding schools — rather than in schools or offices where community mixing dilutes the signal.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp, and Vivian Balenkei
insights.so_what: Names the specific customer segments where a vendor can generate defensible outcome data first — the segments to watch for the category's first credible ROI case studies.

insights.claim: Community-level far-UVC benefit should follow a sigmoidal curve where early adopters see sublinear returns because they still catch illness from uncovered spaces, with suppression only taking off past a critical coverage threshold.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Sublinear early returns mean the ROI pitch to first adopters is structurally weak — a classic coordination problem that argues for subsidy, code mandates, or a single large anchor buyer rather than organic bottom-up sales.
insights.quote: the first few adopters are going to see you know sublinear benefits because you know you maybe you install it in your office and nobody gives each other the flu in your office but then your kids school doesn't install install anything

insights.claim: Elementary and middle schools would deliver the largest health benefit because they are extremely poorly ventilated and children are immunologically naive, but parental caution means early school rollouts will happen in private or specialty schools rather than public ones.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The highest-value segment is not the first-addressable segment; go-to-market realistically starts with occupational settings and private institutions, delaying the biggest social returns.

insights.claim: Universities are a front-runner segment because installations are easier to authorize for adult students than for children, and a competitor has already completed a large install at a Florida university that is reportedly collecting substantial data.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: A competitor's large university install is the nearest-term source of new efficacy data that could re-rate the whole category.

insights.claim: Long-term care chains have naturally incentive-compatible economics for far-UVC because operators are paid per living resident, so a single chain comparing infection counts across locations could trigger rapid intra-chain rollout.
insights.speaker: Patrick McKenzie, host
insights.so_what: Identifies the buyer whose P&L most directly captures the benefit — chain LTC operators are the likeliest first commercial flywheel, with a natural viral coefficient across their own portfolio.
insights.quote: they get paid based on how many residents are still living at the moment

insights.claim: The strongest case for far-UVC is preventing a future pandemic rather than preventing colds, because the more contagious a pathogen is, the more transmission surface area exists to attack.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Inverts the intuitive assumption that mild pathogens are the easy win; the value is concentrated in tail risk, which is precisely the value hardest to monetize commercially.
insights.quote: paradoxically the more contagious something is the more surface area there is to keep it from getting as bad as it as it could get

insights.claim: Legacy 254nm UVC successfully controlled measles outbreaks despite measles having a reproduction number around 20 — the practical extreme of contagiousness — versus COVID-19's R0 of roughly 1-point-something at its worst.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The historical measles precedent is the best existing proof that germicidal UV can break real-world epidemic chains, and implies low coverage in transport hubs could suffice for pandemic suppression.
insights.quote: It is probably the extrema of how contagious a pathogen can even be. I think it has a reproduction number of 20.

insights.claim: Because epidemic growth hinges on whether R0 sits just above or just below 1, a numerically small reduction in transmission is the difference between a pandemic and no pandemic — the same threshold logic as viral k-factor in consumer marketing.
insights.speaker: Patrick McKenzie, host
insights.so_what: Justifies investment in interventions with unimpressive-looking marginal efficacy: near the threshold, small percentage reductions have step-function payoffs.
insights.quote: 1.08 08 means that something goes exponential because you know for every uh uh person that is exposed to the thing you get more than one uh people down the line and uh 0.99 fails to go exponential

insights.claim: Far-UVC's decisive structural advantage over vaccines and masking is that it requires almost no individual opt-in — a single building owner or board can unilaterally protect everyone in the space.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Collapses the sales motion from mass persuasion to a small number of B2B decision-makers, and sidesteps the post-COVID political resistance that burdens pharmaceutical interventions.
insights.quote: vaccination requires a lot of people to opt into vaccination. Masking requires a lot of people to opt into masking. If you have, you know, whoever owns a building can decide unilaterally.

insights.claim: The CEO deliberately avoids mentioning pandemics when marketing far-UVC to ordinary people because the audience is collectively traumatized and does not want to hear it, even though pandemic prevention is the highest-value use case.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The best value proposition is unsellable, forcing the category to be marketed on weaker cold-and-flu claims — a marketing constraint that directly slows the rollout of a tail-risk hedge.
insights.quote: when I talk to people about this, I I really avoid mentioning the pandemic. Uh because yeah, people do not do not want to hear it.

insights.claim: The window to install far-UVC is before the next pandemic, since crash deployment efforts during an outbreak will be far less effective than infrastructure already in place.
insights.speaker: Patrick McKenzie, host
insights.so_what: Frames far-UVC installation as a pre-purchased option on the next outbreak — the value is realized only if bought early, which is exactly why markets underinvest in it.

themes.theme: Objections, failure modes and downside scenarios

insights.claim: The main way far-UVC fails is if airborne disease transmission turns out to be overwhelmingly short-range, leaving the technology critical only for pandemics — where nobody will pay for prevention — and commercially unviable for everyday illness.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: This is the explicit bear case named by the company's own scientist: the technology works but the business does not, because tail-risk prevention has no near-term ROI story.
insights.quote: people hate paying for prevention. It's a lot easier to sell someone something if you can tell them like you're going to benefit from this in the next year

insights.claim: A typical far-UVC install delivers the equivalent of one air change every two minutes, translating to 90% reduction of coronavirus or influenza in the air in about eight minutes and 99% in about fifteen.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Sets the physical boundary of the product's usefulness: it beats shared-air exposure over 30-60 minutes but does nothing against a two-foot face-to-face dose, defining which venues are worth targeting.

insights.claim: The hygiene hypothesis objection is wrong as applied to viruses: immune training comes from environmental and commensal bacteria, not clinical illness, and catching viruses such as RSV or measles is neutral to actively damaging to future immunity.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Neutralizes the most common objection likely to be raised by school boards and parents — the key adoption blocker in the segment with the highest social return.
insights.quote: it is purely just bad to catch a virus and get sick. You know, you might not be able to prevent it, but you would still you would rather it not happen to you at all.

insights.claim: The chief scientist suspects long COVID is not special and that many common viruses carry unmeasured long-term sequelae, meaning society may be chronically suffering from something like 'long flu' without a name for it.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: If correct, the true economic cost of routine viral illness is far higher than measured sick days, systematically understating the ROI on all air-quality interventions.
insights.quote: I have a strong suspicion that long COVID, for example, is not special in that like quite a lot of viruses have long-term squiggle

insights.claim: Far-UVC is uniquely reversible as an infection prevention measure — you turn the lamp off and exposure ends — unlike pharmaceutical interventions whose effects cannot be withdrawn once administered.
insights.speaker: Patrick McKenzie, host
insights.so_what: Reversibility is a genuine risk-management argument that should lower the evidentiary bar regulators and institutions demand relative to drugs.

insights.claim: Indoor microbiome disruption from widespread far-UVC is probably a non-issue because surface-dwelling bacteria are extremely hardy and UVC is much less effective on surfaces than in air — though this has not been explicitly studied.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: A named unstudied gap that a hostile study or advocacy group could turn into a headline risk for the category.

themes.theme: Buyer politics and the corporate ROI channel

insights.claim: Formal far-UVC studies are extremely vulnerable to a heckler's veto because one uncomfortable participant can stop IRB approval, whereas a building owner who simply installs the technology can be studied afterward without that vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Explains why the evidence base will come from retrospective analysis of voluntary commercial installs rather than RCTs — investors should not wait for a randomized trial that may never be run.
insights.quote: You just need one person who is just not totally comfortable with it and the IRB will never let you do it.

insights.claim: In office deployments, resistance typically comes from the building manager weighing the spend rather than from employees, with adoption often substantively driven by employee demand.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: The sales objection is budget, not ideology — which means price reduction, not persuasion, unlocks the office channel.

insights.claim: The apolitical commercial wedge is large employers of highly paid workers who internalize the cost of employee sickness, with Aerolamp specifically trying to reach whoever at Google owns employee health so the decision becomes a bottom-line calculation rather than a public health campaign.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Names the single most plausible anchor customer archetype; a Google-scale deployment would be the category's watershed reference account.
insights.quote: they don't need to have a campaign that's like convincing the average person about these interventions. They just need to do the math and say, "Oh, we think this will benefit Google on the bottom line, right?"

insights.claim: A significant share of the economic cost of common colds is caregiver absenteeism rather than direct absenteeism, because children get sick far more often than adults.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Means the corporate ROI case for far-UVC runs through schools and daycares, not just the office — employers may rationally fund installs in facilities they do not own.
insights.quote: significant part of the economic costs of you know just colds are are actually you know caregiver absenteeism rather than direct absenteeism

insights.claim: Finance firms moved early on ventilation and filtration during COVID without any state mandate, demonstrating that private companies will unilaterally buy clean air when they see a business case.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Precedent that the private, non-mandated channel can move fast — the question is price point, not willingness.

insights.claim: The Aerolamp CEO argues against home purchase at $500 because most households have too little disease transmission for the cost-benefit to work, reserving the case for the immunocompromised or for homes at a $100 price point.
insights.speaker: Misha Gerovich, CEO of Aerolamp
insights.so_what: A CEO talking customers out of buying signals that the consumer channel is not the near-term revenue driver, contradicting the episode's own promotional framing that listeners should buy lamps for their homes.
insights.quote: I think most private homes don't like the costbenefit analysis is not really in the favor of getting one just because there's not that much disease transmission.

insights.claim: The chief scientist partially dissents from her own CEO on homes, arguing far-UVC is worth owning as an occasional-use appliance — switched on when hosting guests around newborns or immunocompromised family members — analogous to a kitchen ventilator.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Reframes the consumer SKU as an event-mode device rather than always-on infrastructure, which is a materially different and cheaper product spec.
insights.quote: it's less something that you might maybe have on all the time, but maybe something, you know, it's it's sort of like the ventilator in your, you know, your your kitchen

insights.claim: Far-UVC is complementary rather than competitive with filtration and ventilation, but meeting a clean air standard in auditoriums, lecture halls and gyms would be cost-prohibitive for most buildings without it.
insights.speaker: Vivian Balenkei, chief scientist at Aerolamp
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific building types where far-UVC is not optional but the only economically feasible compliance path — the highest-conversion segment if a clean-air standard is ever mandated.
insights.quote: auditoriums, lecture halls, gyms, it would be really really difficult to meet the clean air standard for these spaces without UVC. Essentially cost prohibitive for most buildings.
